core_obligations: Normalize X over the perfect closure and descend the resulting morphism of finite presentation to a finite subextension, noting that the descended morphism is geometrically normal because the base changed one is (proof lines 5001-5008).
Increase the finite subextension so that the descended morphism is finite, using descent of finiteness (proof lines 5009-5010).

Increase the subextension again so that the dense open over which the normalization is an isomorphism onto the reduced fibre descends, together with the closed immersion property of the morphism over it (proof lines 5011-5021).

Conclude from the finiteness and the closed-immersion behaviour over a dense open that the descended morphism is the normalization of X_{k'}, which is therefore geometrically normal over k' (proof lines 5022-5023).
proof_roadmap: Descend the normalization from the perfect closure (proof lines 5001-5008).
Descend the dense open and the closed immersion over it (proof lines 5011-5021).
Identify the descended morphism as the normalization (proof lines 5022-5023).
difficulty_reason: For an algebraic k-scheme X, the lemma produces a finite purely inseparable extension k' such that the normalization of X_{k'} is geometrically normal over k' (statement lines 4993-4998). The proof spreads the statement out over the perfect closure of k: normalizing X over the perfect closure gives a morphism, which descends to a finite presentation morphism over some finite subextension, and the descended morphism is already geometrically normal (proof lines 5001-5008). The remaining work is to keep increasing k' until the descended morphism has the two properties that make it a normalization: finiteness, by descending the finiteness of the normalization morphism, and closed-immersion behaviour over a dense open, by descending a dense open on which the normalization is an isomorphism onto the reduced fibre and then descending the closed immersion property (proof lines 5009-5021). The author then reads off that the descended morphism is the normalization (proof lines 5022-5023). The claim is H2: no new construction, but three successive descents along a filtered colimit that must be ordered correctly, with the finite subextension chosen at each step.
